title: stakeFor adds an onlyMigrator gate that the plan explicitly says should not exist
description: The plan's 'NFTStakerV2 deltas / stakeFor' section states verbatim: 'No authorisation gate — anyone can call `stakeFor` provided they own the NFTs to deposit. The deposit requirement (`safeTransferFrom` from `msg.sender`) prevents griefing.' The implementation gates `stakeFor` with `onlyMigrator` (line 521). This is a tightening of access, not a loosening, but it is still a deviation from the documented design and it (a) blocks any third party (e.g., a future helper, a UI batch contract, an EOA donating NFTs to a beneficiary) from staking on someone's behalf, and (b) introduces the same migrator-role trust surface flagged in ECON-01 and ECON-02. The plan's reasoning ('the deposit requirement prevents griefing') is sound: the caller pays the NFTs, so there is no economic griefing vector. Adding the `onlyMigrator` gate centralises an action the plan modelled as permissionless.
impact: Once the migration window closes (no migrator needed) the staker contract retains a `migrator` slot that is the sole address able to call `stakeFor`. Owner can clear it via `setMigrator(address(0))`. If they forget, the migrator retains write access to the staker's user mapping even though no helper is needed anymore. Magnitude: no direct fund loss; the issue is that the on-chain trust model (which the user can read by inspecting code) does not match the documented trust model. Anyone who calls `stakeFor` from a non-migrator address gets a misleading 'caller is not migrator' revert, suggesting an authorisation rule the plan did not intend.
recommendation: Either (a) remove `onlyMigrator` from `stakeFor` to match the plan ('anyone with the NFTs can deposit on a beneficiary's behalf'); or (b) update the plan to reflect the implemented restriction and document why permissionless `stakeFor` was rejected. If (b), also document the operational requirement to call `setMigrator(address(0))` when the migration window closes so the role does not linger.
attack_scenario:
Not an attack scenario per se — this is an intent-vs-implementation mismatch. The implementation is more restrictive than the plan, which is the safer direction, but the mismatch still warrants either a code change or a plan update so the documented trust model matches what users can verify on-chain.

One secondary concern: with onlyMigrator gating, the plan's 'restrict stakeFor to brand-new beneficiaries' open question (point 2 of 'Open Questions') becomes moot in practice — the migrator is trusted not to call stakeFor for existing beneficiaries. But there is no explicit on-chain check; if a buggy migrator calls stakeFor for an existing user, the pending is settled at the OLD price (which is what the user wants) but the test `test_stakeFor_existingBeneficiary_paysPendingToBeneficiaryNotMigrator` confirms the routing is correct. So the open question is closed by trust, not by code.
